title: Havana
description: Capital and largest city of Cuba
wiki_lead:
Havana ( hə-VAN-ə, US also  hə-VAH-nə; Spanish: La Habana [la aˈβana] ) is the capital and largest city of Cuba. The heart of La Habana Province, Havana is the country's main port and commercial center. It is the most populous city, the largest by area, and the second-largest metropolitan area in the Caribbean region. The population in 2021 was 2,142,939 inhabitants, and its area is 728.26 km2 (281.18 sq mi) for the capital city and 8,475.57 km2 for the metropolitan zone. Its official population dropped to 1,749,964 inhabitants by the end of 2024.
Founded in 1519 by the Spanish Empire, Havana overtook Santiago in the mid-16th century due to the geostrategic advantages of its harbor, becoming the capital of the island in 1552. It became a fundamental place for the Spanish colonial empire in the Americas, and a stopping point for galleons returning to the Iberian Peninsula, and walls and forts were built to protect it from naval attacks. Havana is the seat of the Cuban government and ministries, the headquarters of various businesses and home to more than 100 diplomatic offices. In 2009, the city had the third-highest income in the country.
Contemporary Havana can be described as three cities in one: Old Havana, Vedado and the newer suburban districts. The city extends mostly westward and southward from the bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and which divides into three main harbors: Marimelena, Guanabacoa and Antares. The Almendares River traverses the city from south to north, entering the Straits of Florida a few miles west of the bay.
Havana attracts over a million tourists annually, 1,276,627 international tourists in 2010, a 30% increase from 2005. Old Havana was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Havana is noted for its history, culture, architecture and monuments. As typical of Cuba, Havana has a tropical climate.

Etymology
In 1514, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded the town of San Cristóbal de la Habana, which means 'Saint Christopher of the Habana'. It has been theorized that the name is derived from Habaguanex, the chief of a local Taíno-speaking tribe about whom little else is known.
In Spanish, the name was commonly written as Havana or Hauana, as found in historical documents. The spelling "Habana" with a "b" began to be used more frequently starting in 1798, and it became the standard form by 1821.
When Habana was adapted into English, the ⟨b⟩ was switched to a ⟨v⟩ because of a linguistic phenomenon known as betacism, which is an assimilation of the voiced bilabial plosive and voiced labiodental fricative sounds that occurs in most modern Spanish dialects. Usage of the word Havana in literature understandably peaked during the Spanish–American War, but it also represents a type of cigar, a color, and a type of rabbit as well as the city. Havana is the prevailing name for the city found in English-language dictionaries.


History


16th century


Beginnings
Diego Velázquez originally founded Havana in 1514, on the opposite coast, 69 km (43 mi) south of its current location. An early map of Cuba drawn in 1514 places it at the mouth of the Mayabeque River, now the town of Batabanó. This settlement failed, primarily due to the low and swampy nature of the land around the river. All attempts by the Spanish to establish a settlement in this area ultimately failed.
Between 1514 and 1519, the Spanish established the first settlements on the northern coast of Cuba near present-day Havana. One of them was called La Chorrera, on the current site of the Tower of La Chorrera, next to the mouth of the Almendares River. This settlement was in a better location than the first on the southern coast, as the surrounding land was at a higher elevation and the landscape was less marshy. La Chorrera eventually became the neighborhoods of Vedado and Miramar.

grok_lead: Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba, located on the northwestern coast of the island nation in the Caribbean Sea, serving as its primary political, economic, and cultural center. Founded on November 16, 1519, by Spanish conquistador Diego VelÃ¡zquez de CuÃ©llar as San CristÃ³bal de la Habana, the city rapidly grew into a vital Atlantic port for Spanish colonial trade, facilitating the shipment of goods and silver from the Americas to Europe, while its fortifications protected against pirate attacks. Old Havana, the historic core, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982 due to its intact Baroque and neoclassical architecture, urban layout, and defensive system, preserving a snapshot of colonial urbanism despite subsequent neglect. The metropolitan area has an estimated population of 2,156,000 as of 2025, representing about one-fifth of Cuba 's total inhabitants, though official figures have fluctuated amid emigration driven by economic pressures. Under the communist regime established after Fidel Castro's 1959 revolution, Havana transitioned from a prosperous pre-revolutionary hub of tourism, commerce, and nightlife âbolstered by U.S. tiesâto a showcase of ideological control, with landmarks like the Capitolio repurposed and private enterprise curtailed, leading to visible decay in housing, roads, and utilities. The city's economy, once vibrant, now faces acute contraction, with Cuba's GDP over 10% below 2018 levels in 2024, exacerbated by collapsing state industries, chronic energy blackouts exceeding 20 hours daily in parts of Havana, uncollected garbage, and shortages of food, medicine, and fuelâoutcomes rooted in centralized planning inefficiencies, mismanagement, and suppressed market mechanisms rather than solely external sanctions. Despite restoration efforts in tourist zones, much of the infrastructure crumbles from deferred maintenance under fiscal constraints, highlighting the causal disconnect between resource allocation dictated by political priorities and empirical needs for productivity and investment. Havana remains a cultural beacon, blending Afro-Cuban rhythms, tobacco heritage, and resilient street life, yet its defining modern challenge is the tension between preserved colonial grandeur and the stagnation induced by one-party rule.
